questions.q: What does creating a bin from a measure do?
options: Groups the measure's values into equal-sized ranges, producing a new discrete dimension field
Deletes the original measure from the data source
Automatically builds a dashboard filter with no further configuration
Converts the measure into a parameter
questions.explain: Binning takes a continuous measure and groups its values into equal-sized ranges (like $0-999, $1,000-1,999), producing a new field — marked as a dimension — that you can use like any other field.

questions.q: What is the single biggest factor controlling what shape a distribution reveals?
options: Bin size — too wide collapses the shape into a few bars, too narrow creates dozens of near-empty, noisy bars
The color palette applied to the histogram
Whether the field is called a dimension or a measure
The order of fields on the Marks card
questions.explain: Bin size is the main lever: too wide loses the interesting shape, too narrow produces noise. There's no universal right answer — you tune it to reveal the shape of that specific measure.

questions.q: How do you turn a raw bin field like Sales (bin) into a labeled segment such as Low/Medium/High?
options: Build a group (from Lesson 59) that combines several bins into each labeled segment
Bins automatically come with Low/Medium/High labels built in
You must delete the bin and start over with a calculated field
Segmentation is not possible with bins in Tableau
questions.explain: Segmentation reuses the grouping mechanism from Lesson 59 — you group several adjacent bins together and rename the group "Low," "Medium," or "High," turning raw bin values into business-meaningful labels.

questions.q: What kind of field does Tableau produce when you bin a measure — a dimension or a measure?
options: A dimension — binning converts the continuous measure into a discrete field
It stays a measure, just with a smaller range of values
It becomes a parameter automatically
It becomes a calculated field with no data type
questions.explain: Binning converts a continuous measure into a discrete dimension, which is why a binned field like Sales (bin) can go on Rows or Columns the same way Category or Region can.

questions.q: What real-world segmentation model is described as bin-then-group applied to three measures?
options: RFM (Recency, Frequency, Monetary) customer segmentation
A join between two fact tables
A Level of Detail FIXED expression with no bins involved
A Tableau Server permission model
questions.explain: RFM segmentation bins each of Recency, Frequency, and Monetary value, groups each bin field into a small number of labeled tiers, then combines the three tier fields into one composite customer segment.
